subsection: 5. Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration

notes.h: Key terms: ethnic group, race and religion
notes.b: These three categories overlap but are not the same, and migration can bring all three into contact.
points: An ethnic group shares culture, language, ancestry, traditions or religion.
A race is a group classed by physical traits; race is a social idea with no biological basis for ranking people.
Religion is a shared system of belief and practice, and it can cut across ethnic and racial groups.
A multi-ethnic society contains several ethnic groups; a multicultural society is one in which those groups keep distinct cultural practices.
Racism is prejudice or discrimination based on race or ethnicity.
Xenophobia is fear or hostility towards foreigners; Islamophobia is prejudice against Muslims.
Segregation is the clustering of migrants in particular areas, either by choice for support, cheap housing and chain migration, or because discrimination forces them there.
Assimilation is the adoption of the majority culture by migrants.
Integration is the joining of migrants to society while they keep some of their own culture.
Multiculturalism is the acceptance of several cultures as equal within one society.

notes.h: How ethnic, racial and religious issues arise
notes.b: These are the general mechanisms; each applies in the case studies below.
points: Competition for jobs, housing and services, especially in recessions, and fear that wages are undercut.
Visible difference, such as skin colour or dress like the hijab, makes minorities targets of prejudice.
Religious practice in public space (places of worship, dress, halal food, holy days and faith schools) can clash with secular or majority-religion norms.
Residential segregation and concentration in deprived areas reinforce poverty and separation.
Language barriers in schools, work and services.
Political exploitation by far-right and anti-immigration parties and movements, and misinformation on social media.
Second-generation issues: children born in the host country may face discrimination and conflict over identity.
Positive outcomes include cultural enrichment through food, music, sport and festivals, new places of worship, intercultural schools and mixed marriages.

notes.h: Case study: Ireland's growing diversity and religious change
notes.b: Ireland moved from a mostly white, Catholic society to a diverse one from the 1990s.
points: Census 2022: about one in five people (just over 1 million) were born outside Ireland, and about 630,000 were non-Irish nationals (about 12%).
The largest non-Irish groups are Polish, UK, Indian, Romanian, Lithuanian and Brazilian.
Census 2022: about 69% of people were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016.
Census 2022: about 14% had no religion, up from about 10% in 2016.
Census 2022 counted about 82,000 Muslims, about 100,000 Orthodox Christians and about 33,000 Hindus.
The Islamic Cultural Centre of Ireland is in Clonskeagh, Dublin.
About 9 in 10 primary schools are under Catholic patronage, so religion once decided many school admissions.
East Wall, Dublin: protests from November 2022 against housing international protection applicants in a former office building.
Dublin riot, 23 November 2023: after a knife attack on children outside a school on Parnell Square, buses, a Luas tram and shops were burned and looted.
Arson attacks on several buildings proposed for asylum accommodation (2023 to 2024).
Racism and hate crime accompany these tensions, and the protests show how hostility can turn to violence.

notes.b: Irish policy combines equality law, an integration strategy and anti-racism measures, with specific reforms to schools and recognition of Travellers.
points: The Employment Equality Act 1998 and the Equal Status Act 2000 prohibit discrimination on nine grounds, including race, religion and membership of the Traveller community.
The Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 is an earlier law against hatred.
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission was established in 2014.
The Migrant Integration Strategy ran from 2017 to 2020.
The National Action Plan Against Racism was published in March 2023.
The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 gives tougher sentences for crimes motivated by hatred of a protected characteristic.
The Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 removed the baptism barrier, so most Catholic primary schools can no longer use religion to decide admissions.
Educate Together, a multi-denominational school body founded in 1984, runs schools open to all faiths and none.
Irish Travellers were formally recognised by the State as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.

notes.h: Ireland: evaluation and the Traveller community
points: The legal framework is strong, but the 2022 to 2023 protests show that hostility persists.
Direct provision isolates applicants in rural centres, and this works against integration (see the notes on Migration policy in Ireland and the EU).
The Traveller community is an indigenous Irish ethnic minority, not a migrant group; it is included here only as part of Irish ethnic policy.
About 33,000 Travellers were counted in Census 2022.

notes.b: France has a large Muslim population and a strict model of secularism, and it follows an assimilation approach.
points: Post-war immigrant labour came from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal; large-scale Algerian migration followed the Algerian War of Independence (1954 to 1962) and Algeria's independence in 1962.
France has the largest Muslim population in western Europe.
Laïcité, the principle of strict separation of religion and state, dates from the 1905 law.
A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, in state schools.
A 2010 law banned face coverings, such as the burqa and niqab, in public places, in force from 2011.
Banlieues are segregated high-rise estates on the edge of cities, with high unemployment.
The October to November 2005 riots began in Clichy-sous-Bois, a Paris banlieue, after two teenagers died fleeing police; they spread across France and a state of emergency was declared.
June 2023 riots followed the police shooting of a 17-year-old in Nanterre.
The Charlie Hebdo attack in January 2015 and the Paris attacks of 13 November 2015 (130 killed) were followed by rising Islamophobia.
The National Front, founded in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, was renamed the National Rally (Rassemblement National) in 2018 under Marine Le Pen.

notes.h: Case study: Germany and Turkish guest workers
points: A recruitment agreement with Turkey was signed in 1961, and recruitment of guest workers (Gastarbeiter) stopped in 1973.
Guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and brought their families.
Germany long denied them citizenship, and segregated districts formed, such as Kreuzberg in Berlin, which has a large Turkish community.
The 2000 citizenship law gave citizenship to children born in Germany to long-resident foreign parents.
The 2024 reform allowed dual citizenship generally and shortened the residence requirement.
About 3 million people of Turkish origin live in Germany (2020s).
The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), founded in 2013, grew after the 2015 refugee arrivals on an anti-immigration platform.

notes.h: Case study: Britain and the Windrush generation
points: The Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury in June 1948 with passengers from the Caribbean.
Caribbean migrants faced racism in housing and work.
The Notting Hill riots in London in 1958.
The Race Relations Act 1965 was the first UK law against racial discrimination.
The Windrush scandal of 2018: long-settled Caribbean-born residents were wrongly detained, denied services or deported because they lacked documents.

notes.h: Case study: Northern Ireland and the Plantation of Ulster
notes.b: The Plantation was a historic migration whose religious legacy still divides Northern Ireland.
points: The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, after the Flight of the Earls (1607); land taken from Catholic Irish was settled by Protestant colonists from Scotland and England.
Centuries of religious and political division followed, leading to the Troubles from the late 1960s to 1998, in which about 3,500 people were killed.
The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998.
Census 2021 (Northern Ireland): about 46% Catholic and about 43% Protestant and other Christian.
Most children attend schools of their own community, and peace walls still divide some Belfast neighbourhoods.
The Roma are about 10 to 12 million people in Europe (Council of Europe estimate) and Europe's largest ethnic minority.
The Roma originated in northern India and migrated to Europe about 1,000 years ago.
The Roma have faced discrimination in housing, education and employment, and segregated schooling in parts of central and eastern Europe.
France expelled Roma to Romania and Bulgaria in 2010, which drew EU criticism.
France's assimilation model treats all citizens alike and collects no official ethnic statistics.
Ireland's approach rests on equality law and an integration strategy.
Germany moved from excluding guest workers from citizenship to citizenship reform in 2000 and 2024.

questions.prompt: Examine how ethnic and religious issues can arise as a result of migration.
questions.model: Issues arise through competition for jobs, housing and services, visible difference, religious practice in public space, residential segregation, language barriers, political exploitation and second-generation identity conflict. In France, laïcité shapes the response: the 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the headscarf, in state schools, and the 2010 law banned face coverings in public places. Segregated banlieues of high-rise estates, with high unemployment, were the setting for the October to November 2005 riots, which began in Clichy-sous-Bois, and for the June 2023 riots. Terrorist attacks in 2015 were followed by rising Islamophobia, and the National Rally has exploited anti-immigration feeling. In Ireland, religious change has been rapid: Census 2022 showed about 69% Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016, with about 14% of people having no religion. Most primary schools are under Catholic patronage, so religion decided many admissions until the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 removed the baptism barrier. Racism and hate crime appeared in the East Wall protests from November 2022 and the Dublin riot of 23 November 2023, which followed a knife attack on children outside a school and in which buses, a Luas tram and shops were burned and looted. Government responses include the Employment Equality Act 1998, the Equal Status Act 2000, the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (2014), the Migrant Integration Strategy, the National Action Plan Against Racism (2023) and the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024. Evaluation: issues arise from circumstances, discrimination and politics rather than from migrants themselves, and the reforms show that policy can reduce them, although the protests show that hostility persists.

questions.prompt: Describe and evaluate government policy in Ireland on ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
questions.model: Ireland's equality law covers discrimination on nine grounds, including race, religion and membership of the Traveller community, under the Employment Equality Act 1998 and the Equal Status Act 2000, and the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 is an earlier safeguard. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission was established in 2014 to enforce these protections. The Migrant Integration Strategy ran from 2017 to 2020, and the National Action Plan Against Racism was published in March 2023. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 gives tougher sentences for crimes motivated by hatred of a protected characteristic. School policy changed through the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018, which removed the baptism barrier, and through Educate Together, founded in 1984 as a multi-denominational body. Irish Travellers were recognised as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017. Evaluation: the legal framework is comprehensive, and school admissions reform addresses one long-standing barrier. However, the East Wall protests from November 2022 and the Dublin riot of 23 November 2023 show that hostility persists, and direct provision, which isolates asylum applicants in rural centres, works against integration. Policy has been strongest on law and schools and weakest where housing and community pressures meet migration.

questions.prompt: Migration can lead to racial and religious tension. Discuss with reference to one European country other than Ireland.
questions.model: Germany is the example. A recruitment agreement with Turkey signed in 1961 brought guest workers (Gastarbeiter), who were recruited until 1973. Guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and brought families, so the Turkish community became established, with Kreuzberg in Berlin a district where it is large. Germany long denied these long-term residents citizenship, which fed segregation and tension. The 2000 citizenship law gave citizenship to children born in Germany to long-resident foreign parents, and the 2024 reform allowed dual citizenship generally and shortened the residence requirement. About 3 million people of Turkish origin live in Germany. Racial and religious tensions were sharpened by the 2015 refugee arrivals, when Germany received the largest number of asylum seekers in the EU, and by the rise of the Alternative für Deutschland, founded in 2013, which grew after 2015 on an anti-immigration platform. Evaluation: tensions arose because of exclusion, segregation and political exploitation rather than because of migration alone, and the citizenship reforms show that policy can reduce them.
